title: Aggregometry Pre-analytics, Granule Disorders and Scott Syndrome
summary: Why light transmission aggregometry needs citrated platelet-rich plasma and not EDTA, how long aspirin should be stopped before platelet function testing, the normal platelet count, and the platelet disorders that change granules (gray platelet syndrome, δ-storage pool disease) or the procoagulant surface (Scott syndrome).

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 37 Hits 8 (normal platelet count; aspirin before aggregation studies), 12 (gray platelet syndrome and storage pool deficiencies), 13 (Scott syndrome), 14 (aggregometry needs citrated plasma) and Exam Trap 4 (EDTA or aspirin before aggregometry). Checked against Magnette 2016, Boknäs 2019, Alessi 2020, Dupuis 2020, Szanto 2022, Gachet 1993 (abstract only), Lee 2014, Jourdi 2022, Gunay-Aygun 2011, Glembotsky 2021, Palma-Barqueros 2021, Nurden 2021, Toti 1996 (abstract only) and Weiss 2009 (abstract only). The ISTH 2013 LTA recommendations (Cattaneo 2013) could not be read: the publisher page returned HTTP 403. Corrections: one pre-analytical guidance advises stopping aspirin at least 10 days before platelet function sampling, not 5–7 days (register flag rv-aspirin-washout-platelet-testing); “aggregometry requires citrated plasma” holds for LTA but whole-blood impedance aggregometry often uses hirudin (register flag rv-aggregometry-anticoagulant-method); sources describe Scott syndrome as low prothrombin consumption with high residual serum prothrombin, and none read states the direction of the serum prothrombin time (register flag rv-scott-serum-pt-direction). Not taught: the Number Vault table (only its platelet-count row is covered), α-SPD as a separate named entity beyond gray platelet syndrome.

objectives: State the anticoagulant and handling requirements for light transmission aggregometry and explain why EDTA is unsuitable.
Apply the drug-withdrawal guidance for aspirin and other NSAIDs before platelet function testing.
Recall the normal platelet count and the platelet-count limits that affect aggregometry.
Distinguish gray platelet syndrome, δ-storage pool disease and Scott syndrome by defect, genetics and laboratory clue.

scenes.title: Three aggregometry requests
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three platelet aggregation requests reach the coagulation bench. (1) The blood arrived in a lavender-top EDTA tube. (2) The patient took aspirin yesterday. (3) A woman with heavy bleeding after surgery has normal aggregation curves, but her serum still contains a lot of prothrombin after clotting. Question token: “Which result can you trust?”

cues.text: Three platelet aggregation requests arrive. The first sample came in an EDTA tube. The second patient took aspirin yesterday.
The third patient bled heavily after surgery, yet her aggregation curves look normal, and her serum still holds a lot of prothrombin after clotting.
Which of these results can you trust, and what is the third patient missing?

scenes.title: What light transmission aggregometry needs
scenes.altText: Schematic: a light-blue sodium citrate tube feeding a platelet-rich plasma (PRP) cuvette. Card 1: light transmission aggregometry (LTA) uses citrated PRP, from blood drawn into 0.109 or 0.129 M sodium citrate. Card 2: PRP is spun at 200–250 g for 10 minutes without the rotor brake; samples rest at least 15 minutes at room temperature, testing is finished within 3–4 hours, and pneumatic tube transport is avoided. Card 3: the normal platelet count is 150–450 × 10⁹/L; the ISTH guidance cautions that precision may suffer when the PRP count is below 150 × 10⁹/L, and one guidance lists a count below 100,000/µL as a rejection criterion for platelet aggregation.

cues.text: Light transmission aggregometry, the reference test for platelet function disorders, is run on citrated platelet-rich plasma, from blood drawn into 0.109 or 0.129 molar sodium citrate.

Platelet-rich plasma is spun at two hundred to two hundred and fifty g for ten minutes, with no rotor brake. The sample rests at least fifteen minutes at room temperature, testing is finished within three to four hours, and the sample never travels by pneumatic tube.

The normal platelet count is one hundred and fifty to four hundred and fifty times ten to the ninth per litre. The ISTH guidance warns that precision may suffer when the platelet-rich plasma count falls below one hundred and fifty.
One laboratory guidance lists a platelet count below one hundred thousand per microlitre as a reason to reject a sample for platelet aggregation.

scenes.title: EDTA and aspirin wreck the test
scenes.altText: Schematic: GPIIb-IIIa drawn as two joined blocks that split apart in an EDTA tube. Card 1: EDTA treatment causes an irreversible loss of platelet aggregability because it irreversibly dissociates the GPIIb-IIIa complex (shown at 37 °C and alkaline pH). Card 2: aspirin acetylates cyclooxygenase; one pre-analytical guidance advises stopping irreversible platelet inhibitors such as aspirin at least 10 days before sampling, and reversible ones such as other NSAIDs at least 3 days before, if possible, and recording every drug taken in the week before testing. Card 3: when drugs cannot be stopped, their effect must be considered when interpreting results. Card 4: whole-blood impedance aggregometry is often run on hirudin, not citrate.

cues.text: EDTA is the wrong tube. Treating platelets with EDTA causes an irreversible loss of aggregability, because it pulls apart the GPIIb-IIIa complex, the receptor that links platelets through fibrinogen.

Aspirin acetylates cyclooxygenase. One pre-analytical guidance advises stopping irreversible inhibitors such as aspirin at least ten days before sampling, and reversible drugs such as other NSAIDs at least three days before, if possible.
Record every drug taken in the week before testing. If a drug cannot safely be stopped, interpret the result with that drug in mind.
Citrate is not universal, though. Whole-blood impedance aggregometry is often run on hirudin, because responses to ADP can be artificially enhanced in the low-calcium environment of citrated blood.

scenes.title: Granules and the procoagulant surface
scenes.altText: Card 1, gray platelet syndrome (GPS): autosomal recessive, NBEAL2 mutations, absent or markedly reduced α-granules, large pale grey platelets with macrothrombocytopenia; electron microscopy confirms; vitamin B12 is often raised and marrow fibrosis may develop. Card 2, δ-storage pool disease (δ-SPD): dense granules (calcium, serotonin, adenine nucleotides) deficient; Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome adds oculocutaneous albinism; aggregation defects are often moderate and about 25% of δ-SPD patients show no defect. Card 3, Scott syndrome: autosomal recessive, ANO6 (TMEM16F) scramblase; activated platelets fail to expose phosphatidylserine, so tenase and prothrombinase cannot assemble and thrombin generation falls; aggregation and secretion largely normal; clue is low prothrombin consumption, with high residual prothrombin in serum; confirmed by annexin V flow cytometry. Hook answers card.

cues.text: Gray platelet syndrome is autosomal recessive and caused by NBEAL2 mutations. The platelets lack most or all of their alpha granules, so they look large and grey on the smear, with a low count. Electron microscopy confirms it. Vitamin B12 is often raised, and marrow fibrosis can develop.

Dense-granule storage pool disease is a lack of the small granules that hold calcium, serotonin and adenine nucleotides. In Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome it comes with oculocutaneous albinism. Aggregation defects are often only moderate, and about a quarter of patients show none.

Scott syndrome is autosomal recessive, caused by ANO6, a calcium-activated scramblase. Activated platelets fail to expose phosphatidylserine, so the clotting complexes cannot assemble on them. Aggregation is largely normal. The clue is poor prothrombin consumption, leaving high residual prothrombin in serum, and flow cytometry with annexin V confirms it.
Back to the hook. Patient one: recollect in citrate. Patient two: stop aspirin first if safe, or interpret with it. Patient three: think Scott syndrome.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “An EDTA tube is fine for aggregometry” (✓ EDTA irreversibly dissociates GPIIb-IIIa; recollect in sodium citrate for LTA); “Aspirin stopped a day or two ago won’t matter” (✓ one guidance advises stopping aspirin at least 10 days before sampling, if possible); “Normal aggregation rules out a platelet disorder” (✓ Scott syndrome aggregates largely normally, and about a quarter of δ-storage pool patients show no defect).

cues.text: Trap one: an EDTA tube is fine for aggregometry. No: EDTA pulls apart GPIIb-IIIa. Recollect in sodium citrate.
Trap two: aspirin taken a day or two ago will not matter. No: one guidance advises stopping it at least ten days before sampling, if it is safe.
Trap three: normal aggregation rules out a platelet disorder. No: Scott syndrome aggregates largely normally, and about a quarter of dense-granule patients show no defect.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “LTA: citrated PRP, never EDTA · aspirin off ≥ 10 days if safe”, “Gray: no α-granules · HPS: no dense granules · Scott: no PS exposure”.

cues.text: Collect platelet aggregation samples in sodium citrate rather than EDTA, stop aspirin ideally at least 10 days before testing when that is safe, and remember that gray platelet syndrome lacks alpha granules, Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome lacks dense granules and Scott syndrome fails to expose phosphatidylserine.

props.label: LTA: citrated PRP, never EDTA · aspirin off ≥ 10 days if safe
Gray: no α · HPS: no dense · Scott: no PS exposure

explanation.what: Plain language: platelet aggregation testing is easy to spoil before the sample reaches the analyser. The wrong tube (EDTA) permanently breaks the receptor platelets use to stick together, and aspirin, an irreversible platelet inhibitor taken in the days before testing, blocks one activation pathway. Some inherited platelet disorders hide from the test: platelets may lack their storage granules, or may aggregate normally but fail to provide the surface on which clotting factors work. Scientific terms: light transmission aggregometry (LTA), platelet-rich plasma (PRP), sodium citrate, EDTA, GPIIb-IIIa (αIIbβ3), cyclooxygenase (COX), multiple electrode (impedance) aggregometry, hirudin, gray platelet syndrome (GPS), NBEAL2, α-granules, δ (dense) granules, δ-storage pool disease (δ-SPD), Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome (HPS), Scott syndrome, ANO6/TMEM16F scramblase, phosphatidylserine (PS), tenase, prothrombinase, prothrombin consumption, annexin V.
explanation.why: A false abnormal aggregation result can lead to a wrong diagnosis of a platelet function disorder, and a false normal one can miss a real bleeding disorder. EDTA causes an irreversible loss of aggregability; aspirin is an irreversible platelet inhibitor; Scott syndrome has largely normal aggregation, and in δ-SPD aggregation is often only moderately abnormal and normal in about 25% of patients, so other tests (residual serum prothrombin, annexin V flow cytometry, electron microscopy) are needed.
explanation.measure: LTA: citrated PRP (0.109 or 0.129 M sodium citrate); PRP spun at 200–250 g for 10 min without brake; rest ≥ 15 min; complete within 3–4 h; no pneumatic tube. Platelet count normal 150–450 × 10⁹/L; ISTH caveat for PRP counts < 150 × 10⁹/L; one guidance rejects counts < 100,000/µL for aggregation. Drugs: irreversible inhibitors (aspirin, thienopyridines) stopped ≥ 10 days and reversible NSAIDs ≥ 3 days before sampling, if possible; record drugs from the prior week. GPS: EM shows absent or markedly reduced α-granules. δ-SPD: dense-granule count by EM; ~25% have normal aggregation. Scott: residual serum prothrombin high; annexin V binding by flow cytometry reduced.
explanation.differs: GPS (α-granules missing, large grey platelets, macrothrombocytopenia, NBEAL2) vs δ-SPD (dense granules missing; Hermansky-Pudlak adds oculocutaneous albinism and a typically normal platelet count) vs Scott syndrome (granules and aggregation largely normal; the defect is phosphatidylserine exposure). LTA on citrated PRP vs whole-blood impedance aggregometry, often on hirudin.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the correct tube for aggregometry and what EDTA does, how long to hold aspirin before testing, the normal platelet count, which granule is missing in gray platelet syndrome versus Hermansky-Pudlak, and the disorder with normal aggregation but defective procoagulant activity.

questions.stem: Light transmission aggregometry is requested, but the blood was collected in an EDTA tube. What is the best action?

options.text: Recollect the blood in sodium citrate
options.rationale: Correct. LTA is performed on citrated platelet-rich plasma; EDTA causes an irreversible loss of platelet aggregability.

options.text: Run the test and report the results with a comment
options.rationale: Incorrect. EDTA irreversibly dissociates the GPIIb-IIIa complex, so aggregation responses would be falsely abnormal.

options.text: Add calcium to the EDTA plasma and run the test
options.rationale: Incorrect. The loss of aggregability after EDTA treatment is described as irreversible, so the sample must be recollected.
Incorrect. The sample type is wrong for LTA; recollecting in citrate is the fix, not dropping agonists.

questions.stem: A patient on daily low-dose aspirin is referred for platelet function testing. Their physician says aspirin can safely be stopped. According to the pre-analytical guidance taught in this lesson, when should the sample be taken?

options.text: At least 10 days after the last dose
options.rationale: Correct. The guidance advises stopping irreversible platelet inhibitors such as aspirin at least 10 days before sampling, if possible.

options.text: At least 3 days after the last dose
options.rationale: Incorrect. Three days is the minimum given for reversible inhibitors such as other NSAIDs, not for aspirin.
Incorrect. Aspirin acetylates cyclooxygenase and is an irreversible inhibitor, so one day is far too short.

options.text: Timing does not matter if the arachidonic acid channel is skipped
options.rationale: Incorrect. The guidance asks for drugs to be stopped, or for their effect to be considered when results are interpreted.

questions.stem: A woman with bleeding after surgery has a normal platelet count, normal platelet aggregation and normal granule secretion. Her serum contains high residual prothrombin after clotting, and her activated platelets bind little annexin V on flow cytometry. Which disorder fits best?

options.rationale: Correct. Scott syndrome (ANO6) prevents phosphatidylserine exposure; aggregation is largely normal, and the clue is high residual serum prothrombin, confirmed by reduced annexin V binding.
Incorrect. Gray platelet syndrome shows large grey platelets with macrothrombocytopenia and absent α-granules.
Incorrect. Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome is a dense-granule deficiency with oculocutaneous albinism; the defect here is phosphatidylserine exposure.
Incorrect. Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GPIIb-IIIa deficiency) gives absent or markedly reduced aggregation to agonists such as ADP and collagen, with ristocetin spared; aggregation is normal here.

EDTA causes an irreversible loss of platelet aggregability by irreversibly dissociating GPIIb-IIIa (at 37 °C, alkaline pH).

Aspirin acetylates COX; irreversible inhibitors stopped ≥ 10 days and reversible NSAIDs ≥ 3 days before platelet function sampling, if possible; record prior-week drugs; otherwise interpret with the drug in mind.
Whole-blood impedance aggregometry often uses hirudin; ADP responses can be enhanced in low-calcium citrated blood.
GPS: autosomal recessive, NBEAL2, absent or markedly reduced α-granules, large grey platelets, macrothrombocytopenia, EM confirms, raised vitamin B12, marrow fibrosis may develop.
δ-SPD: dense granules (calcium, serotonin, adenine nucleotides) deficient; HPS autosomal recessive with oculocutaneous albinism; aggregation often moderately abnormal and ~25% show no defect.
GPIIb-IIIa (αIIbβ3) links platelets through fibrinogen bridges; Glanzmann thrombasthenia gives absent or markedly reduced aggregation to multiple agonists except ristocetin.

Scott syndrome: autosomal recessive, ANO6/TMEM16F scramblase, no phosphatidylserine exposure, tenase and prothrombinase cannot assemble, aggregation largely normal, high residual serum prothrombin (low prothrombin consumption), annexin V flow cytometry.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 37 Hit 8 and Exam Trap 4 say aspirin must be stopped 5–7 days before aggregation studies. A pre-analytical guidance for haemostasis laboratories (Magnette 2016, citing the BCSH 2011 guideline and the ISTH 2013 LTA recommendations) advises stopping irreversible inhibitors such as aspirin at least 10 days before platelet function sampling, if possible, and reversible NSAIDs at least 3 days. A review table lists 5–7 days as the time to platelet function recovery after aspirin cessation (Jourdi 2022), and one study found arachidonic acid aggregation normalised by 96 hours (Lee 2014), so the reviewer figure may reflect a recovery time rather than the laboratory withdrawal guidance. The lesson teaches the 10-day guidance (register flag rv-aspirin-washout-platelet-testing).

Ch. 37 Hit 14 says aggregometry requires citrated plasma. This holds for LTA on citrated platelet-rich plasma, but whole-blood impedance aggregometry (Multiplate) is commonly run on hirudin, partly because ADP responses are artificially enhanced in low-calcium citrated blood. The EDTA dissociation of GPIIb-IIIa was shown at 37 °C and alkaline pH. The lesson teaches citrate for LTA and notes the hirudin exception (register flag rv-aggregometry-anticoagulant-method).

Ch. 37 Hit 13 says Scott syndrome causes a prolonged serum PT. The sources read describe low prothrombin consumption with elevated residual prothrombin in serum; none states that the serum prothrombin time is prolonged, and an abstract on platelet procoagulant defects describes a defect of this kind as an abnormally short serum prothrombin time (in Bernard-Soulier syndrome). The lesson teaches only high residual serum prothrombin (register flag rv-scott-serum-pt-direction).
